The interview at the Instituto Cervantes
May. The Instituto Cervantes in Bucharest is looking for a Spanish teacher. Ana has sent her CV. Today she has her interview with the director, Mr Martínez.
Good morning, Ms García. Please take a seat. Did you find the institute easily?
Yes, thank you very much. I live quite close.
I’ve read your CV with great interest. I see you’ve been working at a Romanian secondary school for two years.
That’s right. I teach Spanish to students aged fourteen to eighteen. Before that I worked for six years at a language school in Madrid.
And why are you interested in working with us?
Because here I could teach adults, which is what I enjoy most. Also, I’d really love to organise cultural activities: film, literature, cooking…
Interesting. What would you say are your strengths?

I think I’m patient and creative. I know how to adapt to very different students. For example, I had a very shy student who only communicated by drawing, and I managed to get him to speak in front of a hundred people.
Sometimes I find it hard to say no. I get too involved in projects. And my Romanian still isn’t perfect, although I understand almost everything.
That isn’t a problem: Spanish is spoken here. What would your availability be?
I could start in September, when the school year ends. I’d prefer part-time at first, as I have a little girl of a year and a half.
I understand perfectly. Do you have any questions?
Yes. Could you tell me when you’ll make a decision?
At the end of the month. We’ll write to you either way. Thank you very much for coming, Ms García.
“lleva usted dos años trabajando” = you’ve been working for two years
“que acabara hablando” = that he ended up speaking (imperf. subj.)
“a finales de mes” = at the end of the month
In an interview, speak more slowly and clearly than with friends. Pronounce every syllable: “oo-STED”, not “oo-TEH” as you sometimes hear in Madrid.
koo-RREE-koo-loom: rolled rr and the stress on RREE. It’s also written “currículo”.
es-tee-MA-do: the opening formula of formal letters. Don’t use “Querido” (dear, affectionate) in an official letter!
In a formal situation, use “usted” (the formal “you”) ALL the time. Careful: “usted” is conjugated in the third person, and pronouns and possessives change too:
The classic mistake: mixing “usted” and “tú” in the same conversation: “¿Usted tienes…?”. Choose one and stick to it!
In Spain today, “tú” is very widespread, even at work. But in an interview, use “usted” until the other person suggests “tú” (Puedes tutearme).
Me dirijo a ustedes para solicitar el puesto de… / En respuesta a su oferta de…
Cuento con… años de experiencia en… / He trabajado como…
Me interesa especialmente… / Considero que mi perfil se ajusta a…
Adjunto mi currículum. / Quedo a su disposición para una entrevista.
After “Estimado señor” comes a COLON (:), not a comma as in English.
Idiomas: nativo / nivel C1 / nivel B1
In a Spanish CV, language levels are written with the European levels: «Inglés: nativo. Español: nivel B1 (certificado DELE)». You’ll soon be able to write that!

The conditional is your best friend in an interview: podría, me gustaría, preferiría. It sounds polite and confident, without seeming arrogant.

The day of the interview got off to a bad start. At seven in the morning Ana’s phone rang. It was the girl who looked after Rosa Elena two mornings a week: she had a temperature and couldn’t come.

Ana called Mihai, but he was already in theatre. She called Mrs Maria, but she had gone to the doctor’s. She called Elena, but she was in Brașov. At half past eight, Ana had an interview at ten and an eighteen-month-old in her arms.

She thought about cancelling. She wrote the message: “Dear Mr Martínez: I regret to inform you that…”. Then she deleted it. She had been preparing for that interview for a month. She wasn’t going to give up now.

At five to ten, Ana walked into the Instituto Cervantes in her best jacket, with a folder containing her CV and Rosa Elena in the pushchair. The baby was wearing a little blue dress and a strawberry-shaped dummy.
The receptionist, a young woman with glasses, looked at her in surprise. “Are you here for the interview or for a baby class?”
“For the interview,” Ana answered, trying to smile confidently. “There was a little problem with the nanny.”
The receptionist hesitated for a moment. Then she stood up. “Don’t worry. I have two nephews. If you like, you can leave her here with me during the interview.”

Ana was about to accept gratefully when Rosa Elena decided otherwise. She clung to her mother’s neck with all her might and started crying. It wasn’t ordinary crying. It was the crying Mihai called “the fire-engine siren”.

At that moment the door of the director’s office opened. Out came a man of about sixty, with a grey beard and a mustard-coloured tie. He looked at Ana. He looked at the baby. He looked at the receptionist.
Ana wanted the ground to swallow her up. “I’m terribly sorry, Mr Martínez. The person who looks after my daughter fell ill this morning. If you’d rather change the date, I completely understand.”
Mr Martínez looked at her for a few seconds that felt like an eternity. Then he did something unexpected: he crouched down in front of the pushchair and spoke to the baby.
“Hello, young lady. Are you looking for work too?”
Rosa Elena stopped crying at once. She looked with great interest at the mustard-coloured tie. Then she reached out and grabbed it.
“I see,” said Mr Martínez, without freeing himself. “Well, Ms García, I think your daughter has decided the three of us will do the interview. Please, come in.”
The interview lasted forty minutes. Ana answered every question with Rosa Elena sitting on her lap. The baby was quiet almost the whole time, busy messing up the papers on the director’s desk.
When Mr Martínez asked about her strengths, Ana said she knew how to adapt to unexpected situations. The director looked at the baby, who was chewing his pen, and burst out laughing.
“I can see that for myself,” he said.
At the end, when he asked if she had any questions, Ana hesitated. Then she decided to be honest.
“Just one. Will this influence your decision?”
Mr Martínez took off his glasses and slowly wiped them with his tie, which still had a little mark from the dummy.
“Ms García, I’ve been hiring teachers for thirty years. I’ve seen candidates with perfect CVs who didn’t know what to do when a student started crying in class.”
“You arrived on time, with your folder, in spite of everything. You answered my questions with a child chewing my pen. And you lost neither your calm nor your smile.”
“So yes, it will influence my decision. But not in the way you think.”
Ana left the institute without knowing exactly what had happened. It was sunny in the street. Rosa Elena had fallen asleep in the pushchair, still holding the director’s pen.
She called Mihai, who had just come out of theatre. She told him everything, from the nanny’s temperature to the mustard-coloured tie.
“And what do you think the last thing he said means?”
“I have no idea. It could be good, it could be bad.”
A week later, an email arrived from the Instituto Cervantes. Ana opened it with trembling hands.
“Dear Ms García: we are pleased to inform you that you have been selected for the post of teacher. You will be able to start in September, part-time, as you requested.”
“P.S.: Please tell Miss Rosa Elena that she may keep the pen. Consider it her first contract.”

In September, Ana taught her first class at the Instituto Cervantes. It was an adult A2 group, on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. She arrived half an hour early, her heart pounding as on the day of the interview.

The students came in one by one: a nurse who wanted to work in Valencia, a lorry driver who often went to Andalusia, two twenty-year-old students and a retired lady who wanted to read García Márquez in the original.
The last to arrive was a tall man in a grey jacket. He sat in the back row with his arms crossed and greeted her with a serious nod.
It was Mr Dan, Andrei’s father.
Ana took a few seconds to react. “Mr Dan… you already speak Spanish very well. You lived in Chile for five years.”
“I speak the Spanish of bridges,” he answered. “I can say ‘concrete’ and ‘beam’, but I can’t tell my son I’m proud of him. I want to learn the other Spanish.”
Nobody in the class said anything. The retired lady discreetly wiped her eyes. And Ana, who had prepared an activity on introducing yourself, decided to change her plan.

“Very well,” she said, picking up a piece of chalk. “Today we’re not learning how to say our names. Today we’re learning to say what we feel. We’ll start with a very easy sentence: ‘Estoy orgulloso de ti’ (I’m proud of you).”
At the end of the class, Mr Dan was the last to leave. He came up to Ana’s desk and left something on it: a pen with the Instituto Cervantes logo.

“Andrei gave it to me,” he explained. “He says you gave it to him in June, on the day of his Fine Arts exam, for good luck. It’s your daughter’s first contract. And he says that today you need it more than he does.”
